source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events
finding: Founding paper of prospective hindsight. Two experiments varied temporal perspective (event set in the future or in the past) and certainty (event sure or uncertain). In experiment 1 temporal perspective had little influence. Certainty had a strong influence on the explanations. Sure events got longer explanations, more episodic reasons and past tense. Experiment 2 says uncertainty changes the type of explanation, not the time spent.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref). No N, means or tests available to me. The abstract does not contain the popular 30 percent figure.
quote: Explanations for sure events tended to be longer, to contain a higher proportion of episodic reasons
limits: Full text is paywalled (Wiley 403). The abstract names certainty, not the time shift, as the active ingredient. Later writers credit the paper with a 30 percent gain, which the abstract does not state.
agent_relevance: The effect may come from treating the failure as fixed fact, not from imagining a later date. A scaffold prompt should state the failure as already true, not as a possibility.

source: Mitchell et al. (1989) as relayed by Collins, The premortem (blog review)
finding: Secondary reports say imagining an event has already happened (versus may happen) raised the number of reasons generated by about 30 percent. The study counted reasons and did not grade their quality. Klein (2007) restated this as better ability to correctly identify reasons.
numbers: About 30 percent more reasons. N and counts not given in the source I read.
limits: Primary paper not opened, so the 30 percent is secondhand. It sits uneasily with the abstract in a01, where temporal perspective had little influence in experiment 1.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 30 percent as a measured accuracy gain. It is a count of reasons. More reasons may include wrong ones, so a code check must filter them (G2, G3).

source: Klein (2007) Performing a project premortem, Harvard Business Review
finding: The HBR landing page states the method: the team assumes the project has already failed and generates plausible reasons. Aim: make it safe for people who see weaknesses to speak up during planning.
numbers: No numbers on the page I could open.
quote: Team members are often reluctant to voice reservations during the planning phase
limits: Only the summary page was readable. Full text (with the 30 percent claim and two business examples) not opened. Klein is the inventor, so this is advocacy, not a test.
agent_relevance: The stated purpose is social (voice for dissent in teams). A single agent has no reluctance to speak, so part of the original rationale does not transfer.

source: Klein (2015) The pro-mortem method, Psychology Today blog
finding: Klein says he formulated the pre-mortem many years earlier and describes it in Streetlights and Shadows, The Power of Intuition and the HBR piece. Run at project kickoff: imagine months later that the plan failed, each person has two minutes to write reasons. His only empirical claim is that the Veinott study found the premortem reduced overconfidence more than other critiquing approaches. The positive variant (pro-mortem) is described only informally.
numbers: Two minutes of individual writing per person. No sample size or statistics given for the Veinott study.
limits: Self-reported by a co-author of the study. The rest of the support is testimonials, media and one unsolicited email.
agent_relevance: The evidence the inventor himself cites is one conference study. Treat the technique as plausible but weakly tested.

source: Klein, gary-klein.com premortem page
finding: Steps: brief the team on the plan, the leader says imagine the plan has failed, everyone lists threats. Goal: raise the plan's success rate. The page says Klein developed it in 2007 and gives no evidence.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Page links out for further reading. The origin date differs from other accounts (1990s in the implementation paper, see a16).
agent_relevance: The three-step protocol is simple enough to run as one model call after a plan exists.

source: Veinott, Klein, Wiggins (2010) Evaluating the effectiveness of the PreMortem technique on plan confidence. ISCRAM
finding: Main controlled test. University students evaluated a university H1N1 flu lockdown plan under five conditions (including standard critique, pros and cons, cons only, premortem). Premortem cut confidence in the plan more than the other methods, about twice the effect of pros/cons or cons-only, according to secondary reports. Confidence rose most after generating solutions in the premortem condition.
numbers: N = 178. One search-engine summary also said confidence fell about 25 points more than baseline (unverified).
limits: Paper itself not reachable (ISCRAM archive 404 and 503). Numbers are secondhand. Conference paper, not journal. Outcome is confidence, not plan quality or project success.
agent_relevance: A confidence drop alone does not show better decisions. For an agent, lower self-confidence is only useful if it leads to a changed answer that passes a check (G3).

source: Gallop and Bischoff (2016) How to catch a black swan: measuring the benefits of the premortem technique for risk identification. J Enterprise Transformation
finding: Second experiment. Experienced program managers and engineers in teams of 4 to 6 were trained in brainstorming or premortem, then given the same torpedo proximity-fuse scenario for 45 minutes. Premortem teams found more quality risks, made more effective plan changes and caught more black swan risks the historical case missed. A blind expert panel scored quality; above 70 counted as quality.
numbers: N = 101 participants. Effect sizes and p-values not available to me.
limits: Read only through the Collins blog and a Semantic Scholar one-line summary. Paper behind a 403. The comparison is premortem versus brainstorming, not versus a matched-length critique. Teams were trained in each method, so training time may differ.
agent_relevance: Closest human test of risk quality, but the comparison group is brainstorming, not a plain critique at equal tokens (G7).

source: Peabody (2017) Improving planning: quantitative evaluation of the premortem technique in field and laboratory settings. MTU master's thesis
finding: Three experiments extend Veinott. Exp 1: 52 Army cadets in teams on six timed field exercises; premortem teams had fewer fouls and less fixation, with no change in planning or execution time. Exp 2: 72 individuals judged their own group's engineering plan, premortem versus worst-case scenario; no significant difference in number of reasons and solutions, but different category distributions. Exp 3: 82 people judged a complex unfamiliar plan face to face; premortem produced more reasons than worst-case, and groups made more solutions than individuals.
numbers: N = 52, 72 and 82. No test statistics on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only (PDF 403). Exp 2 is a near null against a worst-case comparison. Master's thesis, not peer reviewed. The cadet result is on fouls in field games, not real projects.
agent_relevance: A like-for-like rival (worst-case scenario) did about as well in one experiment. Failure-focused prompts in general may carry the effect, not the premortem frame alone.

source: Koriat, Lichtenstein, Fischhoff (1980) Reasons for confidence. J Exp Psych: Human Learning and Memory
finding: Classic precursor. Asking people to list reasons that contradict their chosen answer reduced overconfidence in general-knowledge judgments, while listing supporting reasons did not. Hill (2012) lists it, with Mitchell 1989 and Veinott 2010, as work showing this kind of approach reduces overconfidence.
numbers: No numbers read. Semantic Scholar shows about 1,500 citations.
limits: Not opened; the finding is stated from memory and from Hill's citation. Task was almanac-style questions, not plans.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap rule: before accepting an answer, ask for reasons it may be wrong. Fits the check-on-signal design if the trigger is a disagreement signal.

source: Hoch (1985) Counterfactual reasoning and accuracy in predicting personal events. JEP: LMC
finding: Early work on imagining reasons for alternative outcomes and its effect on prediction accuracy. Found by a Crossref lookup; I could not retrieve its abstract or results.
numbers: Not read. Semantic Scholar shows about 410 citations.
limits: Not opened. Treat as a pointer only.
agent_relevance: Possible source on how explaining alternative outcomes changes forecast accuracy. Read before using.

source: Hill (2012) Cognition in the woods: biases in probability judgments by search and rescue planners. Judgment and Decision Making 7(4)
finding: Experiment with 32 adult males with search-planning experience. They gave probabilities for where a fictional lost person is. Planners who first unpacked the residual hypothesis (five ways the person left the search area) raised their estimate that the person was outside the area, versus those who unpacked the focal hypothesis. This is support-theory unpacking, in a field setting close to naturalistic decision making.
numbers: N = 32. Change scores F(1,28) = 4.753, p = .038, partial eta squared = .145. Residual-unpack group raised the 'rest of world' estimate by over 4 percentage points. Overall means stayed .81 (search area) and .18 (rest of world).
limits: Small N, all male, fictional case. The experience effect was not significant: 5 of 8 highly experienced planners who unpacked were in the residual condition, 3 of 16 low-experienced showed unpacking.
agent_relevance: Listing specific failure routes moves probability judgments toward the failure side. A scaffold must expect this: enumerating failure stories inflates failure probability beyond the base rate (G5).

source: Hill (2012), subadditivity result
finding: 25 of 32 subjects (78 percent) showed subadditivity: the summed probabilities of the unpacked parts exceeded the probability given to the whole. This is the mechanism by which a premortem lists many failure causes and the total feels too large.
numbers: 78 percent (25 of 32). Focal group: sum of five segments M = 1.07 (SD .33) vs original M = .82 (SD .14), t(15) = 3.14, p = .007. Residual group: sum M = .72 (SD .58) vs original M = .19 (SD .13), t(15) = 3.72, p = .002.
limits: Sums above 1.0 for the focal group show raw incoherence. Fictional scenario.
agent_relevance: If the agent lists failure causes with probabilities, normalise in code so they sum to one (G5). Do not read the raw sum.

source: Hill (2012), discussion of prospective hindsight
finding: The discussion says a prospective-hindsight approach was found by several researchers to cut overconfidence in a focal hypothesis (cites Mitchell 1989, Koriat 1980, Veinott 2010). It also warns that so radical a change in procedure could cause underconfidence in the focal hypothesis and make planners abandon the right area too early.
numbers: No numbers for the warning.
quote: could conceivably lead in some cases to underconfidence in the focal hypothesis
limits: The warning is theoretical (cites Griffin and Tversky 2002), not tested in this paper. Hill did not test prospective hindsight.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a failure frame can overshoot. Use it only when a signal says confidence is too high, and compare the result with a held-out check.

source: Nemeth, Brown, Rogers (2001) Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent. Eur J Soc Psych
finding: A rival to the premortem. A prior study found a role-played devil's advocate led to bolstering of the starting view, not divergent thought. In this study authentic minority dissent beat all three forms of devil's advocate on quantity and quality of solutions.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Social setting with groups; not about planning failures. Used in implementation papers to justify the failure frame over devil's advocate.
agent_relevance: Role-played criticism by the same author may bolster the first answer. This matches G4: the generating model critiquing itself is not independent.

source: Posavac et al. (2008) The effect of temporal frame on information considered in new product evaluation. J Consumer Research
finding: Semantic Scholar's one-line summary: the temporal frame effect is attenuated when certainty is primed, implying that uncertainty tied to the future (versus the past) motivates more comprehensive use of available information.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Machine summary only; paper not opened. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Agrees with a01: certainty, not time, may drive the prospective-hindsight difference.

source: Implementation premortem review: Proactive planning for contextual fit: the role of the implementation premortem. Implement Sci Commun 2025 (authors not checked)
finding: Reviews the premortem for health programs. Says Klein developed it in the 1990s (cites Sources of Power, 1998, and the HBR piece). Premises: assume the program has occurred, assume it failed, and have implementers and recipients (not developers) name the causes. States prospective hindsight raises ability to identify reasons for failure by 30 percent (citing Mitchell 1989) and significantly reduces overconfidence (citing Hill 2012).
numbers: 30 percent (relayed). Compared with devil's advocate and pros and cons lists in text only.
limits: Citation chain issue: the overconfidence claim is attributed to Hill 2012, whose paper is a support-theory unpacking experiment (see a11). The 30 percent is again a reason-generation count. No new data.
agent_relevance: An example of claims spreading by citation without new tests. Do not rely on the 30 percent or the overconfidence claim as established.

source: Implementation premortem review, failure frame argument
finding: Argues the failure frame beats devil's advocate because starting from 'already failed' increases prospective hindsight, whereas devil's advocate starts from 'could fail'. Cites social psychology that devil's advocate bolsters the original view. Also argues developers give myopic or inauthentic criticism, so stakeholders should supply the failure causes.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: An argument by citation, not a direct test of failure frame versus devil's advocate in this domain.
agent_relevance: For one agent, a different voice for the failure story is not available. That weakens the 'who speaks' part and leaves only the framing effect.

source: Beidas et al. (2022) Promises and pitfalls in implementation science: learning from a pre-mortem. Implement Sci 17:55
finding: A real use of the pre-mortem as a method. Ten mid-career US implementation researchers did a group pre-mortem and reached consensus on six themes of threat to the field (insufficient impact; over-emphasis on being a legitimate science; evidence-to-practice gap; accessibility vs coherence; timelines; overly complex strategies).
numbers: 10 participants, 6 themes.
limits: Application, not a test: no control, no outcome measure. Method details are in an additional file I did not open.
agent_relevance: Shows the method yields a list of themes, not a measured improvement. Output must still be checked by code before it changes an answer.

source: Uniqueness bias: why it matters, how to curb it, arXiv 2408.07710 (authors not checked)
finding: Finds perceived uniqueness linked to underperformance across a sample of projects, and lists premortems (Klein 2007) with reference class forecasting, similarity-based forecasting and noise audits as ways to take the outside view. The premortem is recommended, not tested.
numbers: 219 projects (uniqueness vs underperformance). No premortem effect size.
limits: The premortem is cited only as Klein 2007.
agent_relevance: Reference-class (outside view) checks sit next to the premortem in the literature. A reference class is code-checkable (a base rate); a premortem is not.

source: Wang, Cao, Lin, Chen (2026) PreFlect: from retrospective to prospective reflection in LLM agents. arXiv 2602.07187
finding: The agent critiques and refines its plan before acting, grounded in planning errors distilled from past trajectories, plus dynamic re-planning. Not named a premortem, but it is the closest agent analogue. On GAIA validation with GPT-4.1 on the Smolagents framework: total 58.18 percent versus 46.06 plain, 49.70 Reflexion, 49.70 Self-Refine. Gemini-2.5-pro: 59.39 versus 50.30 plain. SimpleQA correct: 83 vs 72 plain (GPT-4.1).
numbers: GAIA total, GPT-4.1: PreFlect 58.18; Smolagents 46.06; Reflexion 49.70; Self-Refine 49.70. Level 3: 38.46 vs 19.23. Gemini: 59.39 vs 50.30. pass@1, single run.
limits: Single run per cell, no confidence intervals. Token cost versus baselines not checked in detail. Gains depend on a library of past trajectory errors.
agent_relevance: Best positive agent result for anticipating failure before acting, but it needs a history of past errors, and it runs every time, not on a signal (tension with G1, see a21).

source: PreFlect ablation
finding: Removing the distilled planning-error prior drops GAIA total from 58.18 to 50.30; removing dynamic re-planning drops it to 51.52. Without the prior, level 3 falls from 38.46 to 23.08. The authors say predicting future errors is hard without historical context.
numbers: Total: full 58.18; w/o planning errors 50.30; w/o re-planning 51.52; plain 46.06. Level 3: 38.46 vs 23.08.
quote: predicting future errors is inherently difficult without historical context
limits: Ablation on one backbone (GPT-4.1) and one benchmark. Single run.
agent_relevance: Imagining failure from nothing helps little; imagining it with real past failures helps a lot. This supports giving the agent real failing outputs (G2) rather than free-form invented failures.

source: InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models, arXiv 2510.01569 (authors not checked; Samsung Research affiliation seen)
finding: The model enumerates potential harms, analyses consequences, then answers under mitigation constraints. The authors call it a premortem framework. Tested as prompting, supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on three model families. Gains grow from simple safety multiple choice to open professional-ethics and agentic scenarios.
numbers: Up to 32 percent lower harmfulness than zero-shot and 16 percent over SafetyPrompt. SafetyBench gain 5 to 13 percent; category gains: illegal activities +15.8 percent (N=1,767), physical health +12.5 (N=1,140), ethics +10.0 (N=1,926), mental health +7.9, offensiveness +2.4. Insider-threat: zero harmful actions in 100 trials per seed over five seeds (Clopper-Pearson upper 95 bound 0.030).
limits: Safety target, not general reasoning accuracy. LLM-judge scoring (three judges, one is also the teacher). Training data comes from Gemini-2.5 Pro. The reasoning check on Qwen-3-8B is single seed.
agent_relevance: Evidence that listing harms first helps where downstream consequences matter, and little where the harm is a surface pattern. Safety is not our target; do not assume transfer to puzzles.

source: InvThink controlled direction test (appendix B.2)
finding: The authors tested whether the failure direction matters, by building a forward-direction corpus (PROTHINK, positive-goal enumeration) with the same prompts, depth and token count. After SFT on Qwen-2.5-7B the two models were statistically indistinguishable on safety. Both collapsed into the same refusal behaviour.
numbers: TRIDENT safety rate 1.000 for both; average harmfulness 1.23 (InvThink) vs 1.01 (ProThink). StrongREJECT attack success 0.000 both. XSTest false refusal 0.980 both. 23,063 training targets. Training loss 1.10 vs 1.01.
limits: Null result under refusal-only data at the SFT stage; the authors say it does not settle the question at the GRPO stage or at prompting level. Single seed.
agent_relevance: The most direct test I found of whether failure framing is special. At SFT it was not: structure and tokens may do the work. Our schema must test failure framing against a matched forward critique at equal tokens (G7).

source: InvThink limits and costs
finding: The full SFT+RL pipeline on Qwen-3-8B still over-refuses benign prompts: false refusal rate 0.361 under the default reward and 0.320 with an over-refusal calibration term. Some baselines (chain of thought, tree of thoughts) scored worse than zero-shot on SafetyBench for Gemma-7B.
numbers: FRR 0.361 -> 0.320, correct refusal 0.927 -> 0.920. Gemma-7B SafetyBench: zero-shot 0.72, CoT 0.69, ToT 0.62.
limits: The limitations section says evaluation is on static benchmarks and only one alternative teacher was tried.
agent_relevance: Failure-focused thinking can cause over-caution (G6: never abstain). Any pre-mortem step needs a rule that it cannot lead to refusal or no answer.

source: Bench to the Future 2 (BTF-2) forecasting agents, arXiv 2604.26106
finding: 1,417 pastcasting questions with a frozen document corpus. The authors built a forecaster that beat any single frontier agent (Brier 0.119 vs Opus 4.6 agent 0.130, a 0.011 gap, CI 0.006 to 0.017, N=1,367). Using Tetlock's CHAMPS KNOW dimensions on written rationales, the better forecaster differed mostly in pre/post-mortem analysis (consider why your forecast might be wrong), wildcards and other perspectives. Pre/post-mortem was in the top three of 37.8 percent of its rationales, with much lower rates for the frontier agents.
numbers: Brier: SOTA 0.119; Opus 4.6 0.130; Gemini 3.1 Pro 0.141; GPT-5.4 0.152; mean of four agents 0.125. Cost per question $1.68 vs $0.55 for Opus 4.6. Pre/post-mortem top-3 share 37.8 percent for the best forecaster.
limits: Correlation, not a test: the better forecaster also had a structured rationale format, more cost and an ensemble. The dimension ranking came from a single LLM call (Gemini 3.1 Pro) on rationales. The authors warn of possible overfitting to BTF-2 questions and a single period (Oct to Dec 2025).
agent_relevance: Suggestive that a pre-mortem step appears in better LLM forecasting, but not isolated. Cost is 3 times higher, so an equal-token test is needed (G7).

source: BTF-2 expert review of agent failures
finding: Expert forecasters reviewed the 130 worst questions from the Opus 4.6 agent. In 24 of 130 they found significant strategic reasoning errors, such as treating stated plans as commitments, and arguing an extreme outcome is unlikely, then down-weighting milder outcomes.
numbers: 24 of 130 questions with significant strategic errors; the 130 are the least accurate 5 percent overall plus the least accurate 5 percent versus the best forecaster.
limits: Selected worst cases; human review of traces; not a test of any intervention.
agent_relevance: Names failure types a pre-mortem could target, but a prompt cannot know which apply. Only a signal (disagreement, failed check) should trigger it (G1).

source: A tutorial on prompt engineering: from messy thoughts to AI workflows, arXiv 2609.22249
finding: Recommends a premortem prompt for high-stakes and assumption-heavy tasks: assume the plan has failed; give the failure story, early warning signs, the most likely failure, the most dangerous failure, the biggest hidden assumption, and a revised direction. Says a premortem works better after steelmanning, because a failure story told about a weakened plan finds faults the plan does not have. States it is not a benchmarking study and measures nothing.
numbers: No measured results.
quote: a premortem works better after steelmanning
limits: Practitioner tutorial. No data. The steelmanning claim is a design argument.
agent_relevance: Gives a useful output format and a warning: a failure story told about a straw plan invents faults. Check each named fault with code, not with the same model.

source: Prospective Hindsight: self-calibrating reinforcement learning via prediction-reality gaps, arXiv 2610.02740
finding: Name clash, not the pre-mortem. A training method that adds a signal from the gap between an agent's prediction before feedback and its evaluation after feedback, to upweight surprising samples and improve calibration. Reports gains in task performance and calibration on single-turn and multi-turn tasks.
numbers: I did not extract the numbers.
limits: The text contains no 'premortem' or Mitchell-style prospective hindsight. A training-time method, so outside a scaffold-only design.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence for the pre-mortem. Possible idea: log the agent's pre-answer confidence and compare with the check result to learn when the signal is real (G7).

source: Serrat (2017) The Premortem Technique, in Knowledge Solutions (Springer, ADB)
finding: Practitioner brief. States that assumptions without probabilities create false certainty, and that working backward from failed assumptions broadens the scenarios examined.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Abstract only. A non-research guide for development-agency staff.
agent_relevance: Shows how the method is taught: a planning aid for humans, not an answer-accuracy tool.

source: Survey of arXiv for pre-mortem work (my title and abstract searches, to Nov 2026)
finding: Searches for 'premortem', 'pre-mortem' and 'prospective hindsight' surfaced InvThink (2510.01569), BTF-2 (2604.26106), the prompt tutorial (2609.22249), the uniqueness-bias paper (2408.07710) and the unrelated PH reinforcement learning paper (2610.02740). I found no paper that tests a stand-alone premortem prompt against a plain critique at equal tokens on reasoning accuracy.
numbers: 6 results for 'premortem' (4 relevant to this topic), 4 for 'pre-mortem' (1 relevant), 2 for 'prospective hindsight' (1 name clash).
limits: Title and abstract search of arXiv only; other venues, and papers that use the idea under other names, are not covered. The shared web search budget ran out early.
agent_relevance: An open gap: our agent would be testing this for the first time. Plan an A/B at equal tokens with a code check as the judge.

source: Collins, The premortem (blog review of the evidence base)
finding: Summary of the evidence: the academic literature is thin; Klein 2007 cites only Mitchell 1989, which counted reasons not their quality; Veinott 2010 is a conference paper; three studies in all (Mitchell, Veinott, Gallop) and none measures project outcomes. Klein's listed benefits (early risk identification, counter overinvestment, valuing team intelligence, awareness) and two business examples are anecdotal.
numbers: Three studies in all; 178 students (Veinott), 101 managers and engineers (Gallop).
limits: A practitioner blog, not a peer-reviewed review. Post date not read (year is a guess).
agent_relevance: Matches the SUBFIELDS note that there is no effectiveness evidence at project-outcome level. Still true in the human literature I could open.
